govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PoliticalMorali:
Hundreds of citizens signed this pledge during the Vietnam era. They refused to pay their federal income taxes voluntarily while American forces were used, in their words, in violation of the Constitution, international law, and the United Nations Charter. The pledge names Vietnam and the invasion of the Dominican Republic. It also charges American indifference to crimes committed in the signers' names.

War tax refusal was a disciplined form of protest: sign, refuse, and accept the penalties. A printed pledge with hundreds of names turned private conscience into public record. The document preserves the movement's legal argument in its own words. It also preserves its moral one, that paying for a war is a choice for which each taxpayer answers.
meyer-us4798661-gas-generator-voltage-co:
Stanley A Meyer received United States Patent 4,798,661 on January 17, 1989, for a gas generator voltage control circuit. The circuit watches over the cell in his water fuel cell system. It is one of the later filings in his eight-patent family.

The design senses how much gas the cell is making and adjusts the voltage to match. Meyer wanted steady gas flow without wasting power or overheating the cell. The drawings show the sensors, the control loop, and the safety cutoffs. A patent proves a design was new on paper only. An Ohio court found Meyer's claims fraudulent in 1996.
what-was-it:
Fitz-James O'Brien, an Irish born writer in New York, wrote this tale for Harper's Magazine in March 1859. Its full name adds the words 'A Mystery' to the stark first line. O'Brien died young, in the Civil War, with a small set of tales that still stand tall.

Men in a boarding house seize a beast that no eye can see, and bind it fast. It is strong, it fights, and it can be felt and heard, yet the gaze passes through it as through air. The tale is the first of the unseen beast, a root of a vast line of later tales.
pareto-manuale-economia-politica-1919-it:
Pareto restated his economics compactly in the Manuale di economia politica, here in its 1919 Italian printing. The manual gives his mature theory in short compass. Ophelimity, his coinage for the satisfaction a good gives, replaces the looser term utility. Indifference curves map how a buyer trades one good against another.

From those curves he builds toward the Pareto optimum, the best balance his system allows. The Italian text stands as a documentary original, since no public domain English translation exists. Students use the manual as the clearest door into his economics. Its appendix on math drew praise and complaint alike. The compact force is pure Pareto.
t-mann-konigliche-hoheit:
Mann's fairy-tale prince appears in his original language in Koenigliche Hoheit, the German text of Royal Highness. Klaus Heinrich of the little state of Grimmburg lives inside ceremony until love and American money crack the shell. Behind the charm stands Mann's serious theme: how art and representation shape modern life.

Elegant and ironic, the novel treats its prince's uselessness as a kind of artistry awaiting a purpose. The heiress Imma brings candor and capital in equal measure. Mann keeps the tone light while the questions about duty deepen underneath. German readers can savor the courtly prose exactly as written. The book charms first and argues afterward, a rare order of operations for its author.
griboyedov-verstand-schafft-leiden-woe-f:
Chatsky returns to Moscow full of wit and ideals and finds society stupid, corrupt, and ready to call him mad. Alexander Griboyedov's verse comedy Woe from Wit appears here in German translation as Verstand schafft Leiden. Written in 1824, the play became the masterpiece of Russian drama before Chekhov.

Nearly every line of Griboyedov's verse passed into proverb; Russians quote it the way English speakers quote Shakespeare. Famusov's stuffy household, the silent Molchalin, and Chatsky's blazing monologues fill a single ballroom with a whole society. The comedy circulated in manuscript for years because censors feared it. German readers receive a classic whose home audience knows it by heart. Few national literatures rest so much on one play.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-non-expedit: Non Expedit was the papal ban that told Italian Catholics it was not expedient to vote in the new kingdom's elections. This entry explains its history, its reasons, and its long political shadow. The pope's veto on the ballot box.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-sorba: This biographical entry profiles Paul de Sorbait, an Austrian physician and scholar of the 1600s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-the-her: Peter the Hermit was the fiery preacher whose cry of God wills it launched the First Crusade. This entry traces his preaching, his crusade, and his legend. The apostle of the crusade: his ragged People's Crusade marched to certain disaster.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philipp-veit: Philipp Veit was the Nazarene painter who directed the Städel and adorned Frankfurt's churches. This entry sketches his career, his frescoes, and his school. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-deusd: Deusdedit was the saintly pope of the early 600s, devoted to the clergy. This entry notes his pontificate, his charity, and his sanctity. The father of his priests: his fatherly love formed the young Roman clergy in virtue and holiness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pulpit: The pulpit is the preacher's elevated stand in the church. This entry traces its forms, its carvings, and its history. The throne of the sermon: its winding stairs lift the preaching friar toward heaven itself in carved stone steps of old.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-paul-th: St. Paul the Hermit was the first of the anchorites. This entry traces his flight, his cave, and his legend. The raven's guest in the Thebaid: his dark cave hid the saint in the Thebaid's rocks of Egypt in the 200s.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-abban-the-: St. Abban the Hermit was the solitary of the Irish woods. This entry traces his cell, his austerities, and his cult. The saint of the hidden life: his lonely cell crowned the woods in the 500s' Ireland in the midlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-deusdedit: St. Deusdedit was the archbishop of Canterbury. This entry traces his see, his plague, and his fame. The first English primate: his new see crowned Canterbury in the 655 of the English in the kingdom of Kent in the south.
martin-chuzzlewit: Dickens's 1844 novel of selfishness in all its forms, following young Martin Chuzzlewit from England to a swampy, fraudulent America and back. as-you-like-it: Shakespeare's sunniest comedy: Rosalind, exiled to the Forest of Arden, disguises herself as a boy and coaches her own lover in the art of love. an-essay-on-comedy-and-the-uses-of-the-c: George Meredith's 1877 lecture on what comedy is for: not mere laughter but the civilized exposure of folly. Drawing on Molière and Shakespeare, he argues that the comic spirit is society's immune system. Elegant, demanding, and influential, it remains one of the finest short defenses of humor as a moral force.
five-children-and-it: E. Nesbit's 1902 classic: five children find a grumpy Psammead, a sand-fairy, that grants wishes with disastrous results. Funny, magical, and perfectly plotted, it invented the modern children's fantasy. The book every child should read.
little-dorrit: Charles Dickens's 1857 novel of the Marshalsea prison: Little Dorrit's quiet heroism amid debt, bureaucracy, and the Circumlocution Office. Dark, intricate, and deeply felt, it is his great novel of imprisonment. A masterpiece of social criticism.
the-grand-canyon-of-arizona-how-to-see-i: George Wharton James's guide to seeing the Grand Canyon: trails, viewpoints, and wonder. Enthusiastic and practical, it opened the canyon to tourists. A classic of Western travel. James's enthusiasm for the canyon knew no bounds.

un-ga-res-statement-of-president-rodrigo:
Rodrigo Duterte, president of the Philippines, addressed the United Nations General Assembly for the first time at its seventy-fifth session in 2020. the-herd-boy-and-his-hermit: The Herd Boy and His Hermit, Charlotte Yonge's tale. The boy and the hermit. This book preserves that story. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.

20111-with-those-who-wait:
With Those Who Wait appeared in 1918, a book of wartime waiting and travel in France. One bright scene recalls a party driving through French villages toward dinner. They stop at The Elephant on the quay for evening papers. Then they pass Essommes, with its fine old church, Bonneil, and Romery.

Such calm scenes sit close to the strain of the First World War. Those who wait at home, or near the front, fill these pages. The book blends travel, grief, and hope in a wartime key. Readers get a sense of France in 1918 beyond the trenches alone.
20721-a-little-girl-in-old-detroit:
Amanda M. Douglas wrote popular historical novels for young readers, and her 1902 book sets a girl's story in early Detroit. The opening pages linger on wild vines, deep forests, rivers full of fish, and wild birds. That rich natural world frames a frontier town still close to the woods around it.

Readers meet Detroit through a child's eyes, with daily life set against trade, travel, and a growing settlement. Douglas mixes simple history with warm scenes of home and nature. The book shows how American girls' fiction once taught the past through place and family rather than through battles and dates alone.
19857-the-great-war-as-i-saw-it:
Canon F. G. Scott, a Canadian chaplain, wrote The Great War As I Saw It. Its verse salutes England of fathers and sons alike. A mother's voice called men oversea, the poem says. The blood she gave is the blood they spill for her. Scott served at the front with Canadian troops. His memoir mixes such verse with front-line witness.

Chaplains buried the dead and comforted the living daily. Scott's view runs from billets to dressing stations. He writes as pastor first and soldier second. Canadian readers took the book to their hearts. It stands among the best-known Canadian war memoirs. Its faith and grief are inseparable throughout.
20005-a-narrative-of-the-life-of-rev-noa:
Noah Davis wrote his own life in this narrative, published in 1859. He was born enslaved in Madison County, Virginia, in March 1804. His father John Davis and family belonged to Robert Patten. Patten was a wealthy merchant residing in Fredericksburg. Davis learned the saddler's trade and found faith young. His narrative tells how he bought freedom for himself and his family, member by member.

Davis became a Baptist minister in Baltimore after freedom. He published the narrative to raise money to free his last children. Few slave narratives show the economics of self-purchase so plainly. Prices, wages, and years of saving fill his account. The book is both memoir and fundraising instrument. Its plain facts carry enormous moral weight.
20494-the-shrieking-pit:
The Shrieking Pit is a detective novel by Arthur Rees, set in a lonely part of Norfolk. A pit in the district gives the book its eerie title. Rees opens with a note to local readers who might think they know the ground.

He states that all the personages are fictitious. The scenes lie in a part of Norfolk that many Norfolk people will readily identify. Norfolk police officials appear in the story, but they too are invented. The warning only sharpens the mystery: a real landscape, a strange pit, and a crime that needs a detective's patience.
21266-bird-day-how-to-prepare-for-it:
Charles A. Babcock, superintendent of schools at Oil City, Pennsylvania, started the Bird Day movement. He had noticed children's interest in birds during nature study in the spring of 1894. His 1901 book tells schools how to prepare for a day devoted to birds. The Audubon Society and the Department of Agriculture helped it along.

Chapters cover the movement's history, the value of birds, and the destruction of birds for feathers and sport. Most of the book teaches accurate study of a few common birds, using government illustrations. Babcock believed that once children studied a few birds well, further study would take care of itself.
21451-ben-hadden-or-do-right-whatever-co:
Ben Hadden grows up in an east coast fishing village in W. H. G. Kingston's Ben Hadden, or Do Right Whatever Comes of It. The village crews man the herring boats, among the finest sea boats in England. Ben's father, a godly fisherman, raises him in the same faith.

Hard times strike the family, and Ben is hurt while saving children from a runaway horse. Lieutenant Charlton befriends him and helps his mother, then takes him to sea. Ben hopes to find his lost brother Ned, who has suffered wreck in the Pacific. Faith, rescue, and tales of island missions fill this short Victorian tale.
21462-the-frontier-fort-or-stirring-time:
A Hudson's Bay Company party crosses a wide prairie at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Frontier Fort. Mr Burnett, a head clerk in charge, jokes that their trade will die when settlement comes. Flowers, rose bushes, and waving grass cover the Red River country around them.

The tale builds on fort life in the North-West Territory of British America. Ambushes, shootings, and fast rides fill the action, as Kingston promises stirring times. Traders, Indigenous peoples, and rivals meet on ground where law runs thin. For readers of frontier tales, the book gives a Canadian twin to the western stories of the States.
21795-fred-fearnot-s-new-ranch-and-how-h:
Fred Fearnot, boy hero of the Work and Win weekly, turns from Wall Street to ranching in this story by Hal Standish. It first ran in the magazine on July 4, 1919. Fred has just beaten the brokers who tried to crush him, turning from bull to bear at the right moment. Broker Bellamy, his worst enemy, is left nearly ruined.

Bellamy's nephews hire thugs to beat Fred, and the pair flee New York when the plan fails. Fred and his friend Terry then take up the new ranch of the title. The tale mixes market fights with western management. It is pure dime-weekly momentum: a young hero always one bold move ahead of grown villains.
22080-true-stories-of-wonderful-deeds-pi:
True Stories of Wonderful Deeds offers very young readers short tales of brave and famous acts. Each story comes with pictures and simple words. One tells of the Royal Oak in Shropshire, said to descend from the tree that hid an English king. That king was Charles II, who escaped his enemies in the oak after a lost battle.

Other pieces retell escapes, rescues, and acts of loyalty from history. The book belongs to a Victorian class of gift books for good children. Its lessons are plain: courage, kindness, and faithfulness win praise. For adults it now serves as a sample of how history was first fed to the nursery in story form.
22143-the-panama-canal-conflict-between-:
The Panama Canal Conflict Between Great Britain and the United States of America studies a sharp legal quarrel. When the canal neared completion, America planned to refund tolls to her own coastwise ships. Britain protested that the Hay–Pauncefote Treaty promised equal treatment for all nations. This Cambridge study asks whether refunding tolls breaks that promise.

Its table of contents separates refunding from outright exemption, page by page. The argument is dry, close, and legal, built for scholars of international law. The dispute ended when President Wilson asked Congress to repeal the exemption in 1914. The book remains a precise record of how the canal's first great diplomatic fight was argued.

Joel Chandler Harris published Uncle Remus and Brer Rabbit in 1906, late in his famous series. Harris, an Atlanta journalist, had learned the tales from enslaved storytellers in Georgia. Here a man goes out to his truck patch and finds things missing: a cabbage here, a turnip there, and a mess of beans yonder. He looks round and sees Brer Rabbit's tracks, for Brer Rabbit left his shoes at home and came barefooted.

That theft sets the trickster running through the book. Brer Fox, Brer Bear, and the rest pursue him and lose. Harris's dialect is now read with mixed feelings, but the tales themselves descend from African and Cherokee story stock. The 1906 volume keeps Uncle Remus telling to the end.
